concept.name: Graceful Degradation Tiers

relationships.description: Connects Graceful Degradation Tiers to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Graceful degradation protects core user journeys during traffic spikes or dependency outages by shedding non-essential features (recommendations, live counts, heavy analytics) in prioritized tiers before core paths fail.
spark.keyTakeaway: Classifying endpoints and features into P0–P3 criticality tiers—paired with adaptive load shedding, circuit breakers, and stale-cache fallbacks—keeps checkout and auth at 99.99% availability even at 5x normal load.

concept.whyItMatters: Without deliberate degradation tiers, a failure in a non-critical microservice (such as personalized product recommendations or review aggregation) exhausts thread pools and database connections, dragging down login and checkout in a cascading outage. Graceful degradation turns catastrophic 503 blackouts into invisible, controlled brownouts.
whenToUse: High-traffic consumer platforms (e-commerce, fintech, streaming) facing flash sales, breaking news spikes, or regional dependency outages
Microservice architectures where a critical synchronous path fans out to 5+ optional enrichment services
Cost- and latency-sensitive AI/LLM pipelines that can fall back from expensive frontier models to smaller cached or heuristic responses under load
whenNotToUse: Strictly regulated financial ledger writes, medical dosing, or safety-critical control loops where partial/stale execution is worse than failing closed
Simple single-process CRUD apps with no optional dependencies where standard rate limiting suffices
Masking chronic capacity under-provisioning—degradation is an emergency safety valve, not a substitute for autoscaling
keyPoints: Criticality tiering (P0–P3): explicitly tag every feature and RPC—P0 (auth, payment capture, order placement), P1 (cart, search), P2 (personalized ML ranking, live inventory badges), P3 (reviews, view counters, analytics).
Priority-based load shedding: at the API gateway or Envoy proxy, shed P3 and P2 requests first when CPU, queue depth, or Little's Law concurrency limits cross thresholds.
Fail-open vs. fail-closed boundaries: P0 security/fraud checks fail closed (reject on timeout), whereas P2/P3 enrichments fail open to empty lists or cached defaults.
Stale-while-revalidate & fallback caches: serving 15-minute-old catalog prices or top-selling items from Redis/CDN avoids hammering an overloaded origin database.
Runtime brownout switches: pre-tested feature flags allow on-call engineers (or automated SLO burn-rate triggers) to disable heavy subsystems in <5 seconds without redeploying.

examples.title: Flash Sale Brownout Preserving Checkout at 6x Traffic
examples.scenario: During a major sneaker drop, traffic surged 6x in 90 seconds; the ML personalization service and real-time '12 people viewing this' badge saturated the primary Postgres read replicas.
examples.outcome: Triggering Tier-2 brownout mode disabled ML reranking (falling back to cached category popularity) and dropped live view counters, cutting origin DB CPU from 98% to 52% while keeping P0 checkout success at 99.96%.

examples.title: LLM Support Copilot Falling Back During Provider Rate-Limit Storm
examples.scenario: A customer support portal hit upstream 429 rate limits on its primary reasoning LLM during a billing incident, causing 30-second timeouts across agent dashboards.
examples.outcome: A circuit breaker tripped after 5 consecutive 429s, routing P1 ticket summarization to a smaller low-latency model and serving pre-indexed FAQ snippets for P2 suggestions—keeping agent dashboard p95 under 800 ms.

tradeOffs.pro: Failing open on P2/P3 features keeps the user experience responsive and preserves revenue-generating P0 flows.
tradeOffs.con: If applied accidentally to auth, rate-limiting, or inventory locking, failing open causes security breaches or overselling.

tradeOffs.factor: Static Thresholds vs. Adaptive Concurrency Limits
tradeOffs.pro: Adaptive limits (like Netflix concurrency-limits using Vegas/Gradient2) self-tune to actual downstream latency without manual tuning.
tradeOffs.con: Harder to reason about during sudden traffic shifts than simple static per-tier semaphore caps.

tradeOffs.factor: Stale Cache Fallbacks vs. Live Queries
tradeOffs.pro: Serving stale-if-error data shields databases from retry storms and thundering herds.
tradeOffs.con: Risks showing slightly outdated prices or stock counts until the origin recovers.

failureModes.name: Untested Fallback Path Collapse
failureModes.description: A fallback path (e.g., querying a secondary cache or SQL fallback) is never exercised in steady state; when triggered during an outage, it immediately crashes or OOMs.
failureModes.mitigation: Run regular chaos/game-day drills (e.g., weekly 1% brownout injection in staging/prod) to verify fallback paths handle real traffic.

failureModes.name: Retry Amplification Across Tiers
failureModes.description: When Tier-2 services shed load with 503s, upstream callers blindly retry 3x, turning a 2x spike into 6x pressure on the API gateway.
failureModes.mitigation: Return explicit non-retryable headers or 429 with Retry-After, and disable client retries on P2/P3 optional calls.

failureModes.name: Shared Thread Pool Starvation
failureModes.description: P0 checkout and P3 analytics share the same HTTP worker pool or DB connection pool; hanging P3 queries starve P0 requests.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce bulkheads—separate connection pools, worker queues, and circuit breakers per criticality tier.

failureModes.name: Missing Hysteresis (Flapping Brownouts)
failureModes.description: Automated load shedding turns off P2 features at 80% CPU, CPU drops to 75%, features immediately turn back on, and the system oscillates violently.
failureModes.mitigation: Add hysteresis and cooldown timers (e.g., shed at >80% for 10s, restore only after <60% for 120s).

commonMistakes: Marking every endpoint 'P0 Critical'—if everything is P0, nothing can be shed during an outage.
Placing long 30-second timeouts on optional P2/P3 RPCs inside a P0 request handler with a 500 ms SLO.
Returning HTTP 500 to the user when a non-essential widget (like 'Recommended for You') fails, instead of omitting the widget.
Forgetting to include request priority headers (e.g., X-Request-Priority: P0) so downstream proxies know which traffic to drop first.
Allowing client SDKs to retry shed requests aggressively without jittered exponential backoff and retry budgets.

sections.content:
## The idea

Most distributed systems fail catastrophically not because their core business logic breaks, but because peripheral features consume the same CPU, threads, and database connections under stress. If a 99.95% availability SLO allows only **21.9 minutes of downtime per month**, you cannot afford for an outage in a recommendation engine to take down checkout.

Graceful degradation treats system capacity as a **prioritized budget**. Every request, microservice call, and UI widget is assigned a criticality tier (typically P0 through P3). Under normal load, all tiers execute. As latency climbs or error budgets burn, the system systematically sheds lower-priority work—substituting stale caches, simplified heuristics, or empty responses—so P0 revenue and safety paths remain fast and available.

## Concrete walkthrough

Follow an e-commerce Product Detail Page (`GET /products/sku-904`) during a 4x traffic spike:

1. **Ingress Classification**: The API gateway tags the request `P1` (browsing) while `POST /checkout` is tagged `P0`. Envoy enforces an adaptive concurrency limit based on gradient latency tracking.
2. **Parallel Fan-Out with Tiered Budgets**: The Product Aggregator fans out to four services with strict per-tier timeouts: Catalog Core (`P0`, 120 ms), Pricing (`P0`, 100 ms), Live Inventory Count (`P2`, 50 ms), and ML Recommendations (`P3`, 40 ms).
3. **Brownout Activation**: Origin DB CPU hits 82% for 15 seconds. An automated controller (or on-call engineer) flips the `degrade_tier=2` flag.
4. **Controlled Shedding**: The Aggregator skips the ML Recommendations RPC entirely (returning an empty `recs: []` array) and replaces Live Inventory Count with a CDN-cached boolean (`in_stock: true`, TTL 5 min). Pricing falls back to Redis `stale-if-error`.
5. **Preserved Core**: Total DB queries per page view drop by 65%, p99 page latency stays under 190 ms, and `P0` checkout traffic continues unthrottled.

sections.content:
## Load shedding and concurrency control

Static RPS rate limits are brittle because a database that handles 5,000 simple lookups/sec may collapse at 400 complex search queries/sec. Modern proxies and services use **queue-time and concurrency-based** shedding:

- **CoDel (Controlled Delay)**: Instead of measuring queue length, CoDel measures how long the oldest request has waited in the queue. If minimum sojourn time exceeds a target (e.g., 50 ms) over an interval, it drops incoming low-priority requests immediately (LIFO or priority-ordered).
- **Adaptive Concurrency (Netflix `concurrency-limits` / Envoy)**: Compares short-term `minRTT` against current `RTT` (Little's Law). When queuing inflates latency, the proxy shrinks the max in-flight concurrency window automatically—no static threshold tuning required.
- **Retry Budgets**: Cap client retries at ≤10–20% of total requests so a partial degradation never snowballs into a self-inflicted retry storm.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / Service criticality tiers and fallback matrix
sections.content:
## Service criticality tiers and fallback matrix

| Tier | Examples | Timeout Budget | On Overload / Outage | Failure Mode |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **P0 (Critical)** | Auth, Checkout, Payment Capture | 300–500 ms | Dedicated pool; shed P1–P3 first | Fail closed (explicit 429/503 with backoff) |
| **P1 (Core UX)** | Search, Cart Read, Product Page | 150–250 ms | Serve CDN/Redis stale-if-error cache | Degraded read-only mode |
| **P2 (Enrichment)** | Live Inventory Counts, ML Ranking | 40–80 ms | Circuit-break to heuristic/popular list | Fail open (cached boolean or default sort) |
| **P3 (Optional)** | User Reviews, View Counters, Analytics | 20–40 ms | Drop immediately via brownout flag | Fail open (omit widget / drop telemetry) |

## Failure modes

- **Cascading Thread-Pool Exhaustion**: Calling a slow P3 service synchronously without a bulkhead or short timeout ties up P0 request threads until the entire service crashes.
- **Cold Fallback Stampede**: All pods simultaneously fall back to an uncached secondary query path, crashing the fallback database.
- **Brownout Oscillations**: Turning degradation on at 80% CPU and immediately off at 79% creates violent load spikes every few seconds.
- **Silent Data Corruption**: Accidentally applying fail-open semantics to P0 authorization or idempotency checks during an outage.

## Validating degradation with game days

A fallback path you have never tested in production is a fallback path that will fail during an incident. Mature teams validate degradation continuously:

- **Dark-Launch Brownout Drills**: Weekly automated chaos experiments inject 100% failure or 500 ms latency into P2/P3 dependencies for 5 minutes on 1%–5% of traffic, verifying zero P0 error-budget burn.
- **Synthetic Load Shedding Tests**: Replay 2x–3x peak production traffic in staging with `P0` synthetic probes running alongside `P2/P3` load to confirm `P0` p99 latency remains flat while `P3` sheds cleanly.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Classify every API endpoint and downstream RPC into `P0`–`P3` and propagate priority headers (`X-Request-Priority`).
- [ ] Isolate `P0` thread pools, goroutine worker pools, and DB connection pools from `P2/P3` workloads (bulkheads).
- [ ] Cap `P2/P3` RPC timeouts strictly below the parent `P0` deadline (e.g., 50 ms inside a 300 ms request).
- [ ] Implement runtime brownout feature flags for every heavy ML, analytics, or third-party enrichment.
- [ ] Configure hysteresis (e.g., shed at >80% for 10s, restore at <60% for 120s) and cap client retry budgets at ≤15%.
- [ ] Test every fallback and circuit-breaker path monthly via controlled fault injection.

interviewProblems.title: Graceful Degradation Tiers
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Graceful Degradation Tiers. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Graceful degradation protects core user journeys during traffic spikes or dependency outages by shedding non-essential features (recommendations, live counts, heavy analytics) in prioritized tiers before core paths fail.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: P2/P3 Enrichments applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Fallback & Stale Cache.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Fallback & Stale Cache experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Run regular chaos/game-day drills (e.g., weekly 1% brownout injection in staging/prod) to verify fallback paths handle real traffic.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Classifying endpoints and features into P0–P3 criticality tiers—paired with adaptive load shedding, circuit breakers, and stale-cache fallbacks—keeps checkout and auth at 99.99% availability even at 5x normal load.
Avoid trap: Marking every endpoint 'P0 Critical'—if everything is P0, nothing can be shed during an outage.
Avoid trap: Placing long 30-second timeouts on optional P2/P3 RPCs inside a P0 request handler with a 500 ms SLO.
When to reach for it: High-traffic consumer platforms (e-commerce, fintech, streaming) facing flash sales, breaking news spikes, or regional dependency outages
When to reach for it: Microservice architectures where a critical synchronous path fans out to 5+ optional enrichment services

putItTogether.title: Putting Graceful Degradation Together
putItTogether.summary: Classifying endpoints and features into P0–P3 criticality tiers—paired with adaptive load shedding, circuit breakers, and stale-cache fallbacks—keeps checkout and auth at 99.99% availability even at 5x normal load.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Graceful Degradation before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Triggering Tier-2 brownout mode disabled ML reranking (falling back to cached category popularity) and dropped live view counters, cutting origin DB CPU from 98% to 52% while keeping P0 checkout success at 99.96%.
